claims.text: A US court found Google’s search business to be a monopoly because Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia ruled on 2024-08-05 that Google violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by acting as a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising [Source: ev-1].

witness.reason: claim figures absent from the evidence — untraced: 2

claims.text: The primary theory of harm was "default-distribution deals," where Google paid companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions of dollars to remain their default search engine [Source: ev-1].
Specifically, trial evidence showed that Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021 and gave Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1].

specifics: Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021

claims.text: Judge Mehta determined this conduct was exclusionary because it created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generate scale, which creates data, improves quality, and ultimately protects the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1].

On 2025-08-05, structural remedies were ordered requiring Google to sell its Chrome browser—marking the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000—and prohibiting any future payments for default search placement or revenue-sharing agreements [Source: ev-1].
